opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point is recognizing that the web was built for humans. Everything about it, from how pages are laid out to how search results are ranked to the business model of ads and clicks, assumes a person with eyes, limited time, and maybe ten blue links' worth of patience. Agents are a fundamentally different kind of user. They don't get tired, they can read a thousand pages in the time it takes us to read one, and they don't care about visual layout. What they care about is getting accurate, verifiable, up-to-date information in a form they can reason over.

So my view is that, over time, agents will use the web far more than humans do. I'd guess it'll be orders of magnitude more. If that's true, the web needs a second set of interfaces built for that new primary user. That's what we're trying to build at Parallel: infrastructure that lets agents search, retrieve, and research across the open web in a way designed for how they actually work.

Practically, that means a few things. First, moving from returning links to returning evidence. An agent doesn't need a ranked list of pages. It needs the relevant passages, with provenance, so it can cite and verify what it's relying on. Second, letting agents spend compute on harder questions. Some tasks need a quick lookup. Others need deep research that might take minutes and touch hundreds of sources. We want developers to be able to dial that tradeoff between cost, latency, and quality explicitly, instead of getting one-size-fits-all search. Third, accuracy and calibration. When agents act on information, being wrong is expensive, so we care a lot about benchmarks, confidence, and showing our work.

The piece I think about most over the long term is the economics. The current web runs on human attention: people visit pages, see ads, and that funds the people creating content. If agents become the main consumers, that loop breaks unless we build a new one. I think there's an opportunity, and honestly a responsibility, to make sure the people who create the knowledge on the open web keep getting rewarded, so the web stays open, healthy, and worth reading. If we get that right, agents don't hollow out the web. They make it more valuable than it's ever been.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents searching, retrieving, and researching the web, but does not describe agents activating other agents.

r002.rationale: It discusses agents getting information from the web, but does not predict a shift to notifications triggered by specified actionable changes.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss agents exhausting worthwhile work given available compute or subsequent work depending on newly arriving events or information.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the web was built for humans. Every page, every search engine, every interface assumes there's a person on the other end with a browser, a pair of eyes, and about ten seconds of patience. That worked incredibly well for thirty years. But the web's primary consumer is changing. Increasingly, it's going to be agents, not people, that are pulling information from the web, reasoning over it, and acting on it. And the infrastructure just isn't built for that.

So the first thing I'd say is that agents need a different kind of access than humans do. A person runs one search, skims a few results, clicks around. An agent working on a hard problem might want to issue hundreds or thousands of queries, follow every lead, read full documents rather than snippets, and then reconcile conflicting sources. If you give it a human search engine, you're handing it a tool designed for the wrong user. What we're building at Parallel is essentially web infrastructure where the API is the product, not the webpage. The agent describes what it needs, declaratively, and we go do the work of searching, reading, extracting, and verifying, and hand back something structured.

The second piece is that agents can afford to be far more thorough than people, and the output should reflect that. A human doing research has a budget of attention. An agent has a budget of compute, and compute keeps getting cheaper. So I think you'll see tasks that used to be "google it and read a few pages" turn into deep, multi-step research where the agent is genuinely exhaustive. And that puts a huge premium on the quality of the underlying retrieval, because errors compound. If the agent reads something wrong on step three, everything downstream is wrong. So we care a lot about returning not just answers but evidence, citations, and confidence, so the model can calibrate how much to trust what it got.

The third thing is economics. Right now the web runs on an implicit deal between publishers and search engines: you let me index you, I send you traffic, you monetize that traffic. Agents break that deal, because the agent reads the page and the human never shows up. I don't think the answer is to pretend that's not happening. I think we need new mechanisms where the value agents extract from the web flows back to the people who created the content. Otherwise the web gets worse over time, and agents end up reasoning over a degraded corpus. That's a problem I think about a lot, and I don't think anyone has fully solved it yet.

So if I zoom out: in a few years, I expect most web traffic to be machine-generated, I expect the dominant interface to be APIs rather than pages, and I expect the best agents to be the ones with access to the most reliable, most verifiable, most up-to-date view of the web. Our job is to be that layer.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents searching, reading, and reasoning over the web, but does not say agents activate other agents.

r002.rationale: It predicts more API-based, thorough web research, but does not describe shifting from on-demand requests to notifications about specified actionable changes.

r003.rationale: It discusses cheaper compute and exhaustive research, but does not argue that after agents complete all worthwhile feasible work, subsequent work depends on newly arriving events or information.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll move from a web that people navigate directly to one that agents navigate on our behalf. Today, you search, open a few pages, compare what you find, and decide what to do. An agent needs to do that same work, but often across many more sources and as part of a larger task.

The opportunity with Parallel is to make that interaction work well for agents: help them find relevant information, understand what supports an answer, and bring that information into their reasoning. It’s more than retrieving a page. It’s getting enough reliable context to move the task forward.

I expect that to expand what we use the web for. You could ask questions that would take you hours to research yourself, or have an agent keep track of something as new information appears. The web becomes an ongoing source of knowledge for the work your agent is doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents using the web for research and tracking information, but does not say agents activate other agents.

r002.rationale: It mentions an agent keeping track as information appears, but does not predict a shift from on-demand requests to notifications about specified actionable changes.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe exhausting worthwhile work given available compute or say that later work would depend on newly arriving events or information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the web is going to become a much more important resource for agents. Today, we mostly think of it as something a person navigates—you search, open a few links, read, and synthesize. An agent can do that work on your behalf, but it needs to access information reliably, understand where it came from, and decide whether it has enough evidence to answer your question.

The opportunity with Parallel is to build that interface for agents. Over time, I expect us to move from fairly simple lookups to much more open-ended research, where an agent explores multiple questions, reconciles conflicting information, and brings back a useful result. The user shouldn’t have to prescribe every search or every page to visit. They should be able to describe what they want to accomplish, and the agent should figure out how to use the web to get there.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents researching the web, but does not say agents activate or delegate work to other agents.

r002.rationale: It predicts a shift toward open-ended research, not from on-demand requests to notifications about specified actionable changes.

r003.rationale: It does not describe feasible worthwhile work being exhausted or later work depending on newly arriving events or information.
